sections.section_title: Introduction to RC Low-Pass Circuit Model

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$ measured across the capacitor. Keep the drawing uncluttered, emphasize topology over numerical values, and make the output node obvious.

blocks.text: The canonical RC low-pass circuit is the physical model you will use for the rest of this lesson. It is the source-$R$-$C$-to-ground topology that turns a circuit diagram into an LTI system description.
In the schematic, $v_{in}(t)$ enters a series resistor $R$, the capacitor $C$ goes from the output node to ground, and the output is the capacitor voltage at that same node.

That output convention is the key identification step: $v_{out}(t)$ is the voltage across $C$, so $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$. Keep this topology fixed as the base case; later steps will use the same circuit for the differential equation and the frequency response.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Series Resistor and Shunt Capacitor

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and the output node after the resistor. Keep the drawing uncluttered and pedagogical, emphasize topology over numerical values, and make the output node obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: In the standard RC low-pass circuit, which component is the series resistor and which component is the shunt capacitor?

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same canonical RC low-pass schematic from the tutorial: $v_{in}(t)$ enters a resistor on the signal path, and a capacitor connects from the output node to ground.

To identify the low-pass topology, trace the path from the source to the first component. That first component is the series resistor. Then look at the branch that leaves the output node and goes to ground; that branch is the shunt capacitor.
So in this model, $R$ is the series element and $C$ is the shunt element. That wiring pattern is the RC low-pass model you will carry into the differential-equation and frequency-response steps.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Capacitor Voltage as the Output Signal

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, an output marker across the capacitor, and node labels $v_C(t)$ and $v_R(t)$ to show the capacitor and resistor voltages. Keep the diagram uncluttered and pedagogical, and make the capacitor branch and output marker obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: In the standard RC low-pass circuit, which voltage is the output signal measured across the capacitor?

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same canonical RC low-pass schematic, now with the output marker placed across the capacitor. The cue is the capacitor branch, because the output is measured across $C$, not across the input source or the resistor.
Trace the voltage across the capacitor and name that signal $v_C(t)$. Since the output marker is across the same element, the output signal is the capacitor voltage.
So the output is $v_C(t)$, while $v_{in}(t)$ stays the input and $v_R(t)$ stays the resistor voltage. That output convention is the one you will use in the next RC low-pass steps.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the RC Low-Pass Circuit as an Input-Output Filter

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit annotated with an input arrow at the source, a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and an output arrow across the capacitor. Emphasize signal flow from input to output, keep the diagram uncluttered, and make the system boundary obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: In the standard RC low-pass circuit, identify the input signal, the output signal, and the circuit as an input-output filter.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same canonical RC low-pass schematic, now annotated with an input arrow at the source and an output arrow across the capacitor. The cue is the signal flow from source to capacitor, because the circuit is being read as a two-signal filter.
Mark the source-side signal as the input and the capacitor voltage as the output. The resistor and capacitor together are the system elements that sit between those two signals.

So the model is a driven LTI filter: $v_{in}(t)$ enters on one side, $v_C(t)$ leaves on the other, and the RC network maps one to the other. That system boundary is the interpretation you will reuse in the later differential-equation and frequency-response steps.

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and the output node after the resistor. Keep the drawing uncluttered and pedagogical, emphasize topology over numerical values, and make the output node obvious.

The same standard RC low-pass topology mirrored left-to-right, with the source and output node swapped visually but the resistor still in the signal path and the capacitor still shunting to ground. Keep labels minimal so the learner identifies roles from the wiring, not the layout.

prompt_blocks.text: In the standard RC low-pass circuit shown, which choice correctly identifies the series resistor and the shunt capacitor?
Choose the option that matches the resistor on the signal path and the capacitor that goes to ground.

choice_blocks.text: The resistor on the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor from the output node to ground is the series resistor, and the resistor on the signal path is the shunt capacitor.
The source labeled $v_{in}(t)$ is the series resistor, and the output node is the shunt capacitor.
The resistor on the signal path is the shunt capacitor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the series resistor.
The branch from the output node to ground is the series path, and the resistor on that path is the shunt element.

questions.correct_answer: The resistor on the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the shunt capacitor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Trace the input path from $v_{in}(t)$ to the first component: that resistor is in series. The capacitor branch that leaves the output node and goes to ground is the shunt capacitor.

prompt_blocks.text: In the mirrored RC low-pass circuit shown below, which choice still correctly identifies the series resistor and the shunt capacitor?
The layout is flipped, but the topology is the same. Choose the option that still follows the signal path and the branch to ground.

choice_blocks.text: The resistor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor branch to ground is the series resistor, and the resistor in the signal path is the shunt capacitor.
The source arrow is the series resistor, and the output node is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the resistor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The output node is the series resistor, and the source arrow is the shunt capacitor.

questions.correct_answer: The resistor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Flipping the drawing does not change the circuit roles. The element on the signal path is still the series resistor, and the branch from the output node to ground is still the shunt capacitor.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Capacitor Voltage as the Output Signal

image_slots.image_description: A clean RC low-pass schematic with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, an explicit output arrow across the capacitor, and visible node labels $v_C(t)$ and $v_R(t)$. Keep the circuit uncluttered and make the capacitor branch and output marker obvious.

The same RC low-pass schematic with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$ and a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, with visible node labels $v_C(t)$ and $v_R(t)$ but no explicit output arrow. Keep the capacitor branch visually prominent so the learner must infer that the output is the capacitor voltage.

prompt_blocks.text: Look at the RC low-pass schematic.
Which labeled voltage is the output signal across the capacitor?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output is measured across the capacitor, so the correct signal is the capacitor voltage.
$v_{in}(t)$ is the input, $v_R(t)$ is the resistor voltage, and $i(t)$ or $q(t)$ are not output voltages.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the same RC low-pass circuit, but focus on the signal across the capacitor branch.
Which signal should be treated as the output?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The filter output is the voltage across the capacitor branch, so it is $v_C(t)$.
$v_{in}(t)$ stays the input, $v_R(t)$ stays the resistor voltage, and $i(t)$ is not the output voltage.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the RC Low-Pass Circuit as an Input-Output Filter

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit annotated with an input arrow at the source, a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and an output arrow across the capacitor. Emphasize signal flow from source to capacitor, keep the diagram uncluttered, and make the system boundary obvious.

A clean schematic of the same RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ marked at the source, $v_R(t)$ labeled across the resistor, and $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$ labeled across the capacitor. Emphasize the input-output roles and keep the resistor voltage visible as a distractor.

prompt_blocks.text: In the RC low-pass circuit shown, which statement correctly identifies the input and output signals?
Choose the interpretation that matches the system boundary.

choice_blocks.text: The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_C(t)$, the output is $v_{in}(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_R(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is the capacitor itself, and the RC network is source-free.
The input is $v_R(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.

questions.correct_answer: The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The source-side signal is the input, so it is $v_{in}(t)$. The output is the voltage across the capacitor, so it is $v_C(t)$.
That makes the RC network a driven LTI filter mapping $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_C(t)$, which is the system boundary used later in the lesson.

prompt_blocks.text: In the same RC low-pass circuit, which statement best describes the whole RC network as a system?
Choose the option that treats the circuit as an input-output filter.

choice_blocks.text: It is a driven LTI filter that maps $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$.
It is a source-free element with no input signal.
It is a driven LTI filter whose output is $v_R(t)$.
It is a capacitor-only system that outputs the capacitor itself.
It is a feedback loop in which the output feeds back to the source.

questions.correct_answer: It is a driven LTI filter that maps $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The circuit is driven by $v_{in}(t)$ and produces $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$, so it is not source-free. The resistor and capacitor together form the filter between those two signals.
That is the input-output interpretation the later analysis steps reuse.
